title: Optimization and Generalization: From Token Loss to Reliable Training
summary: Derive the gradients behind language-model training, reason about AdamW and batch size, and distinguish optimization progress from trustworthy generalization.
learningObjectives: Derive softmax cross-entropy gradients and trace a backward pass.
Explain AdamW, bias correction, and decoupled weight decay.
Compute effective batch sizes and correct token-weighted accumulation.
Diagnose training curves while protecting validation and test boundaries.

sections.title: 1. Specify exactly what the optimizer minimizes
paragraphs: An autoregressive model predicts the next token from earlier tokens. Training usually minimizes the mean negative log probability assigned to the observed next tokens. Define the unit of averaging before discussing optimizer settings: a mean over valid target tokens is different from a mean over sequences. Padding and intentionally masked prompt tokens must not contribute to either the numerator or denominator. Otherwise a change in sequence length silently changes the learning problem.

Let z be a vector of dimensionless logits, p its softmax, y the correct token index, and M the number of valid targets. With natural logarithms, token loss is measured in nats and reported mean loss in nats per token. Cross-entropy is sensitive to confidence: assigning the correct token probability 0.8 costs 0.223 nats; assigning 0.01 costs 4.605 nats. Accuracy alone hides this difference. Perplexity is exp(mean loss), provided the tokenizer and evaluation protocol are identical.

For a worked example, use logits [2, 1, 0] and correct class zero. Their probabilities are approximately [0.6652, 0.2447, 0.0900], giving loss 0.4076. Compute the loss through log-sum-exp with the maximum logit subtracted for numerical stability. A library cross-entropy operation expects logits; applying softmax first changes its input semantics and can damage both the objective and numerical behavior.
sections.formula: pᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ); ℓ = −log pᵧ; L = (1/M)Σₜ ℓₜ; perplexity = exp(L)

diagram.title: Confidence errors have unequal costs
diagram.caption: Analytically calculated samples of −ln(p), not measured model results. Probability is dimensionless; loss uses natural logarithms.

sections.title: 2. Backpropagation computes gradients; the optimizer uses them
paragraphs: Backpropagation applies the chain rule in reverse through the executed computation graph. Each operation receives the derivative of the final scalar loss with respect to its outputs, then propagates contributions to its inputs. Contributions from multiple downstream uses are added. Reverse-mode differentiation is attractive when a scalar objective depends on many parameters: it avoids calculating a separate full forward perturbation for every parameter. Saved activations consume memory; checkpointing trades recomputation for less activation storage.

Softmax combined with one-hot cross-entropy gives the compact derivative p minus the target indicator. In the previous example the logit gradient is approximately [−0.3348, 0.2447, 0.0900]. Its components sum to zero, consistent with loss being unchanged when the same constant is added to every logit. A correct-class logit receives a negative derivative, so subtracting the gradient increases that logit.

Consider a binary toy model with scalar input x = 2, logit z = wx, label y = 1, and w = 0. Initially p = 0.5 and the chain rule gives dℓ/dw = (p − y)x = −1. One SGD step with learning rate 0.1 moves w to 0.1. The new logit is 0.2, probability is 0.5498, and loss drops from 0.6931 to 0.5981 nats. This calculation assumes one example, no regularization, and an exact arithmetic update; it is an explanatory derivation, not a training benchmark.
sections.formula: ∂ℓ/∂zᵢ = pᵢ − 1[i = y]; for z = Wx: ∂ℓ/∂W = (p − onehot(y))xᵀ; θₜ₊₁ = θₜ − ηₜgₜ

diagram.caption: All quantities are from the specified one-example calculation. Backward derivatives flow from loss toward w; SGD is a separate final operation.

nodes.detail: x = 2 and w = 0 produce z = wx = 0.

sections.title: 3. Learning rate must respect local curvature
paragraphs: A gradient points toward the steepest local increase under the chosen parameter coordinates. Moving against it helps only if the step remains compatible with local curvature. On the scalar quadratic L(w) = aw²/2, with a positive, SGD without noise obeys w next = (1 − ηa)w. Convergence requires 0 < ηa < 2. At ηa = 2, the parameter alternates without reducing loss; above that threshold it diverges. A neural network is not globally quadratic, but this local example explains why a seemingly reasonable learning rate can suddenly fail.

Set a = 1, w initially 1, and compare η = 0.5 with η = 2.2. After three steps, their losses are 0.0078125 and 1.492992 respectively, even though both always subtract the current gradient. In many dimensions, the largest curvature direction constrains stability while flatter directions progress slowly. Momentum can smooth noisy directions but is not a license to ignore stability. Inspect gradient norms and update-to-parameter ratios alongside loss; an isolated aggregate loss curve cannot reveal which layer is unstable.
sections.formula: L(w) = aw²/2; wₖ = (1 − ηa)ᵏw₀; L(wₖ) = (a/2)(1 − ηa)²ᵏw₀²

diagram.title: Exact quadratic descent versus divergence
diagram.caption: Analytical toy calculation with a = 1 and w₀ = 1; illustrative of curvature, not measured neural-network training. Loss is in arbitrary objective units.

sections.title: 4. AdamW separates adaptive updates from parameter shrinkage
paragraphs: Adam tracks an exponential average m of gradients and an exponential average v of squared gradients. Bias correction compensates for initializing those averages at zero. Dividing the corrected first moment by the square root of the corrected second moment rescales each coordinate according to recent gradient magnitudes. This is a diagonal adaptation, not a full inverse-Hessian calculation. Epsilon prevents division by a vanishing denominator and its placement is part of the algorithm definition.

AdamW applies weight decay directly to parameters, separately from the loss-gradient moments. Adding λθ to the gradient before Adam instead sends regularization through its coordinate-dependent normalization and changes the moment history. The two procedures therefore generally differ. Under the convention below, the per-step shrinkage factor is 1 − ηλ. Parameter groups may exclude bias or normalization parameters from decay, but exclusions are an explicit modeling choice to record and evaluate.

For one coordinate, take θ = 2, g = 0.5, zero initial moments, β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, η = 0.01, and λ = 0.1. The first moments are m = 0.05 and v = 0.00025. Bias correction recovers 0.5 and 0.25, so the adaptive update is approximately 0.01 when epsilon is negligible. Decay subtracts another 0.002, giving θ next approximately 1.988. This also exposes a schedule interaction: cumulative shrinkage depends on the product of all per-step factors, so changing update counts changes effective regularization.
sections.formula: mₜ = β₁mₜ₋₁ + (1−β₁)gₜ; vₜ = β₂vₜ₋₁ + (1−β₂)gₜ²; m̂ₜ = mₜ/(1−β₁ᵗ); v̂ₜ = vₜ/(1−β₂ᵗ); θₜ₊₁ = (1−ηₜλ)θₜ − ηₜm̂ₜ/(√v̂ₜ + ε)

diagram.title: Two different regularization paths
diagram.caption: Elementwise AdamW convention with decay proportional to learning rate. These paths are generally inequivalent for adaptive optimization.

nodes.label: L2 inside Adam
nodes.detail: Use g + λθ to build both moments. The regularization contribution is adapted along with the data gradient.

nodes.label: Decoupled AdamW
nodes.detail: Build moments from g alone. Apply direct shrinkage (1 − ηλ)θ separately from the adaptive gradient step.

sections.title: 5. Batch size changes noise, update count, and memory
paragraphs: If individual example gradients are independent with covariance Σ, their B-example mean has covariance Σ/B. Standard deviation therefore falls as 1/√B, not 1/B. Tokens from the same document are correlated, so raw token counts do not imply that many independent observations. Larger batches can improve accelerator utilization and reduce gradient noise, yet provide fewer updates for a fixed token budget. Beyond a useful batch scale, extra averaging may buy little statistical progress per unit of computation.

Gradient accumulation processes microbatches while holding parameters fixed, adds their gradients, then performs one optimizer step. With eight data-parallel workers, four sequences per worker per microbatch, and eight accumulation microbatches, the effective batch is 256 sequences. At exactly 2,048 valid targets per sequence, that is 524,288 target tokens per update. The formula uses the number of data replicas, not total GPU count when tensor or pipeline parallelism is also present.

Equivalence to a physical large batch requires matching loss weighting and optimizer timing. Suppose two microbatches contain 100 and 300 valid tokens with mean losses 2 and 4. Their correct combined loss is (100×2 + 300×4)/400 = 3.5, not 3. Average gradients with the same token weights. Dropout realizations, batch-dependent layers, and floating-point reduction order may prevent bitwise equivalence. Clear gradients once per effective batch, and step Adam's moments, weight decay, and the scheduler once per actual update.
sections.formula: B_effective = replicas × sequences_per_microbatch × accumulation_steps; Cov(ḡ) = Σ/B under independent sampling; L = Σₖ(MₖLₖ)/ΣₖMₖ

diagram.title: Averaging reduces noise with diminishing returns
diagram.caption: Analytical illustration for independent scalar gradients with variance 1. Real document gradients can be correlated. Standard deviation is normalized to the single-example value.

sections.title: 6. Treat the schedule and numeric policy as part of the experiment
paragraphs: Warmup raises the learning rate from a small starting value while early updates establish useful parameter and optimizer statistics. Subsequent decay reduces update magnitude as training progresses. Cosine decay is one smooth choice, not a universal optimum. Define schedule position in optimizer steps or consumed tokens explicitly. If accumulation doubles, a step-based schedule sees twice as many tokens before reaching the same step; a token-based schedule preserves that aspect of the training budget.

For a toy schedule, warm up to 0.001 over 100 updates, then cosine-decay to zero over the next 900. At update 550, halfway through decay, the rate is 0.0005. If training stops early or extends beyond the planned horizon, revisit the schedule deliberately. Increasing batch size can mimic some noise-reduction effects of decreasing learning rate in particular settings, but it also changes optimizer update counts and need not preserve an AdamW run.

Numeric policy matters just as much as nominal hyperparameters. In mixed-precision training with loss scaling, keep the scale fixed across an accumulated update and unscale before inspecting or clipping gradients. Clip the full accumulated gradient rather than each microbatch independently: clipping is nonlinear. A skipped update after nonfinite gradients should not silently advance a schedule intended to count successful updates. Record precision, overflow counts, clipping frequency, and actual processed tokens with each checkpoint.
sections.formula: For t ≤ W: η(t) = η_max t/W. For W < t ≤ T: η(t) = (η_max/2)[1 + cos(π(t−W)/(T−W))]. Here W = 100 and T = 1000 updates.

diagram.title: Warmup followed by cosine decay
diagram.caption: Analytically calculated illustrative schedule, not measured results. Learning rate is the scalar optimizer coefficient; t counts successful optimizer updates.

sections.title: 7. A better training loss is not a trustworthy evaluation
paragraphs: Optimization asks whether the model fits the selected training objective; generalization asks whether performance transfers to the deployment population. A training-validation gap may reflect memorization, distribution shift, or different measurement conditions. Compare like with like: training-mode dropout, augmentation, and changing data mixtures can make live training loss incomparable to an evaluation-mode pass over a fixed sample. A smooth validation improvement is useful evidence only if the split itself is meaningful.

Split by the unit that must generalize. For a support assistant, tickets from the same customer or copied template may cross a random row split; for forecasting, future records must not influence past predictions. Keep related documents together and audit exact and near duplicates. Fit learned preprocessing on training data only. Validation can guide checkpoint and hyperparameter selection, while a reserved test set measures the final choice. Repeatedly selecting on test results converts that set into another validation set.

A practical experiment should retain data provenance and evaluate representative slices: new customers, longer contexts, rare intents, and later time periods. More data, better filtering, weight decay, dropout, and early stopping address different failure mechanisms; none proves that contamination is absent. If validation loss worsens after an earlier minimum, select a checkpoint using the predeclared validation rule and investigate whether the change exceeds evaluation noise. The illustrative curve below encodes that scenario, not a law that all models eventually overfit.

diagram.title: Checkpoint selection needs held-out evidence
diagram.caption: Invented illustrative curves, not measured results. Both losses use the same tokenizer, masking policy, and evaluation mode. The validation minimum occurs at update 300.

interview.question: An eight-replica language-model run doubles gradient accumulation to avoid memory pressure. Training becomes smoother, but validation worsens at the same reported step. How do you investigate?
interview.answer: First clarify the change: accumulation alone does not lower per-microbatch activation memory; lowering the microbatch size does. Compute the old and new valid tokens per update, then compare checkpoints at matched tokens and compute budgets. If microbatch size was unchanged, accumulation doubled the effective batch and tokens at each step. Verify token-weighted loss reduction, data-parallel averaging, one optimizer and scheduler step per effective batch, and clipping after accumulation. Audit whether the schedule now warms up over twice as many tokens and whether cumulative AdamW shrinkage changed at matched token counts. Compare training and validation in the same evaluation mode, inspect gradient norms and nonfinite events, and verify data ordering and split contamination. Run a controlled batch/schedule comparison before attributing the effect to reduced gradient noise. Select the final configuration with validation and reserve the test set for final assessment.
followUps: When does accumulation equal a physical large batch, and when does it fail?
How would you correctly normalize variable-length sequences across replicas?
Which quantities must a checkpoint preserve for an exact optimizer resume?
What evidence would distinguish overfitting from a changed validation distribution?

pitfalls: Confusing backpropagation, which computes derivatives, with an optimizer, which chooses updates.
Passing softmax probabilities into an API that expects logits.
Averaging microbatch means when valid token counts differ.
Assuming more accumulation reduces the activation memory of an unchanged microbatch.
Advancing weight decay or the scheduler once per microbatch instead of once per intended optimizer update.
Treating repeated test-set selection or duplicate-contaminated validation as evidence of generalization.
checklist: Specify tokenizer, target mask, loss denominator, and units before comparing losses.
Log valid tokens per update, data replicas, microbatch size, and accumulation count.
Record AdamW betas, epsilon, decay parameter groups, and scheduler time unit.
Inspect gradient norms, update ratios, overflow events, and clipping frequency.
Match token or compute budgets when comparing batching and schedules.
Split by document, entity, or time as deployment requires; fit preprocessing only on training data.
Choose checkpoints using a declared validation rule and evaluate the untouched test set afterward.

flashcards.front: What does a language-model cross-entropy of 2 nats per token mean?
flashcards.back: It is the average negative natural log probability of valid target tokens. Its perplexity is exp(2), approximately 7.39; comparison requires the same tokenizer and masking policy.

flashcards.front: What is the derivative of one-hot cross-entropy with respect to a softmax logit?
flashcards.back: pᵢ − 1[i = y]. The correct token receives a negative derivative unless its probability is already one, so gradient descent raises its logit relative to alternatives.

flashcards.front: How does backpropagation differ from gradient descent?
flashcards.back: Backpropagation computes loss derivatives by the chain rule. Gradient descent uses those derivatives to change parameters; the same backward pass can supply AdamW or another optimizer.

flashcards.front: When does gradient descent converge on L(w) = aw²/2?
flashcards.back: For a > 0 and constant learning rate, 0 < ηa < 2 makes the multiplier 1 − ηa have magnitude below one. A larger step can increase loss despite following the negative gradient.

flashcards.front: Why does Adam correct its moment estimates for initialization bias?
flashcards.back: Moments initialized at zero underestimate early magnitudes. Dividing by 1 − βᵗ corrects that initialization effect under the moment estimator's assumptions.

flashcards.front: Why is AdamW not generally equivalent to adding L2 loss to Adam?
flashcards.back: An L2 gradient enters Adam's moment estimates and adaptive normalization. AdamW shrinks parameters separately, preserving a direct decay path independent of the gradient preconditioner.

flashcards.front: With θ = 2, g = 0.5, η = 0.01, λ = 0.1, what is the first AdamW update from zero moments?
flashcards.back: Bias-corrected moments are 0.5 and 0.25. Ignoring epsilon, the adaptive step is 0.01 and decay is 0.002, giving approximately 1.988.

flashcards.front: How does independent-gradient noise change when batch size increases fourfold?
flashcards.back: Covariance falls by four and standard deviation by two. Correlated samples weaken this simple relationship, so token count is not automatically an independent sample count.

flashcards.front: Compute the effective batch for 8 replicas, 4 sequences per microbatch, and 8 accumulation steps.
flashcards.back: 8 × 4 × 8 = 256 sequences per optimizer update. Count data-parallel replicas rather than total GPUs if other parallelism is present.

flashcards.front: Two microbatches have 100 and 300 targets with mean losses 2 and 4. What is the combined mean?
flashcards.back: 3.5, since (100×2 + 300×4)/400 = 3.5. Averaging the means would give 3 and overweight the shorter microbatch.

flashcards.front: Why clip after gradient accumulation and unscaling?
flashcards.back: Clipping is nonlinear, so clipping each microbatch can change the final direction. Loss scaling changes gradient magnitudes, so unscale first to make the threshold meaningful.

flashcards.front: Why specify whether a schedule uses updates or tokens?
flashcards.back: Changing batch size changes tokens per update. An unchanged step schedule can therefore warm up or decay over a different amount of data.

flashcards.front: Why can training-only model fitting still leak evaluation information?
flashcards.back: Preprocessing, duplicate documents, entity overlap, and hyperparameter selection can expose held-out information without directly optimizing model weights on those rows.

flashcards.front: What happens when you repeatedly select models on a test set?
flashcards.back: The test set becomes a selection signal, effectively another validation set. A fresh untouched evaluation is needed to estimate performance of the selected model without that selection bias.
